Photograph: AP US military Three journalists sue Pentagon after being fired from military news outlet Three employees of Stars and Stripes, a government-funded news service, allege they were fired after reporting on USS Abraham Lincoln Robert Mackey Thu 27 Aug 2026 19.33 EDT Last modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 19.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three journalists who were fired by the Pentagon from a US government-funded news outlet sued the Department of Defense in federal court on Thursday, arguing their dismissals were illegal and violated their first amendment rights to free speech. The three journalists were all employees of Stars and Stripes, which their court filing calls “the U.S. military’s independent news source since the Civil War with a long history of editorial independence, free from news management or censorship by military command”. Max Lederer, the news outlet’s former publisher Max Lederer, Erik Slavin, the editor-in-chief, and Lara Korte, Middle East correspondent, allege the defense department and Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, “are attempting to fire Plaintiffs for speaking up as private citizens in support of the press’s freedom to cover military operations, its need to reach all servicepersons, and in retaliation for their publication of a news report on deteriorating conditions aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln during its extended tour of duty in the Mid-East”. Slavin and Korte said they were dismissed for supposed “insubordination” during an interview with CBS News in which they objected to potential censorship by the US military . According to the complaint, no one at the Pentagon took “immediate action” after the interview aired on 5 July. “After all, the anodyne statements endorsing Stripes’ editorial independence were entirely consistent with DoD’s own longstanding insistence on Stripes’ independence,” reads the complaint. The journalists allege that “the spark that moved [the Pentagon] to act” was an 11 August news report about the conditions on the troubled USS Abraham Lincoln , which had been supporting US military operations in the middle east for nearly nine months. “The article broke a major story about deteriorating conditions aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln,” the complaint says. “It reported that the aircraft carrier’s 5,000 Sailors have endured food and water shortages, disrupted mail service, long workdays, and little time off for months on end, and that the long deployment and physical hardships were impacting Sailors’ physical and mental health”. The day after that article was published by Stars and Stripes, the suit contends, Lederer was ordered to fire Slavin and Korte – five and a half weeks after the CBS News interview. Lederer ultimately declined to comply with the order. “Lederer did not deliver the notices,” the suit explains. “Instead, he decided then and there to retire, and informed the Stripes’ staff via email. Mr. Lederer took this step because he did not want to be part of Defendants’ scheme to illegally punish Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte for exercising their First Amendment rights.” Lederer was dismissed shortly after announcing his impending retirement, effective at the end of September. He said the Pentagon had installed a new deputy publisher, an active duty service member, under him at the newspaper without his prior knowledge. “Stripes’ historical editorial independence is critical to its core mission of gathering and providing unbiased, credible journalism to the U.S. military community, particularly servicemembers and their families stationed overseas,” the suit also says. The Pentagon did not immediately return a request for comment on Thursday’s lawsuit. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP Australian Greens Greens gear up for fight with Labor as Sarah Hanson-Young pushes to strengthen laws to rein in big tech Minor party plans to drive a tough bargain in exchange for support for digital duty of care legislation Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy Political editor Sun 11 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 10.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Greens will push Labor to dramatically toughen new laws designed to rein in big tech, calling for individuals to have the right to take platforms to court and win financial compensation. As Labor prepares to introduce its planned digital duty of care laws into parliament this week, the Greens say they will drive a tough bargain in exchange for support, including pushing for fines by the eSafety commissioner to be levied as a percentage of corporations’ global revenue rather than set amounts. The Coalition is opposed to the duty of care plan, giving the Greens the upper hand in negotiations. Their communications spokesperson, Sarah Hanson-Young , said the laws should do more to address the addictive nature of platforms. “To meaningfully change the behaviour of big tech companies, the digital duty of care laws must include the right for Australians who have been harmed online to be able to take legal action and seek compensation for the damage done,” she said. “Enforcement of the digital duty of care cannot be left to the eSafety commissioner alone. “To really put Australians’ online safety at the heart of this reform, individuals and the community need to have the right to take on big tech through a private right of action.” The negotiations will be the first under the new Greens leader, David Shoebridge . He has flagged a tougher negotiating approach than under his predecessor, Larissa Waters, potentially frustrating the government’s agenda in the second half of the year. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Shoebridge is expected to introduce a bill to stop the importation of so-called “pervert glasses” and other wearable technology this week. Labor wants progress on its remaining budget bills, including moves to make tax treatment for trusts less generous. Last month the government said it would legislate the duty of care and establishing fines of more than A$100m for platforms not protecting users from harm. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Anika Wells named on Time100 list as one of ‘world’s most influential rising stars’ after social media ban Read more Popular platforms as well as online games, apps and AI chatbots will be required to protect against specific harms, including pornography; eating disorder content; misogynistic content; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that could cause serious distress, including abuse and bullying. The regulator, the eSafety commissioner, will have the power to issue removal notices to companies, with operators required to document measures taken to address online harms. Users over 16 years of age will also be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content. But Hanson-Young has warned that the proposed fines are too small to change the behaviour of tech giants. “Fines for breaches must be tied to a percentage of global revenue,” she said. “The threat of serious fines and compensation is the only way to force these companies to clean up their act and proactively provide a safe environment for their users.” The communications minister, Anika Wells, will address the National Press Club on Thursday. She has pledged to work constructively with the Greens and any other party to deliver basic safety standards. “We want these platforms to embed safety by design,” Wells said. “Some of them have had 15 years to do it of their own accord. They haven’t, so now we’re going to legislate that they must.” The shadow communications spokesperson, Sarah Henderson, warned on Sunday the duty of care laws could restrict free speech. “At stake is something generations of Australians have fought and died to defend,” she told the Conservative Political Action Conference . “Your freedom of speech questions authority, to challenge government, to expose injustice, and above all, the freedom to disagree.” Explore more on these topics Australian Greens Social media ban Sarah Hanson-Young Australian politics Business Internet safety David Shoebridge news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters

https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuania_ca.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuania calls Moscow court ruling on Baltic resistance figures falsification of history 2026-10-07 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry has called a Moscow court’s decision to recognize more than a dozen Baltic anti-Soviet resistance participants as "accomplices of Nazi Germany" a falsification of history. "This is not the first time Russia has falsified history to smear the Baltic states and our freedom fighters, thus trying to divert attention from its war crimes and other atrocities in Ukraine," the ministry said on Wednesday. According to the ministry, Russia distorts historical facts by relying on biased archival documents and remaining silent about crimes committed by Soviet repressive structures. It said such a campaign was primarily aimed at a domestic Russian audience and sought to indirectly justify its aggression in Ukraine. In the Siberian city of Yakutsk, a memorial dedicated to Lithuanian and Polish deportees was replaced in September by a monument to Russian soldiers killed in the war in Ukraine, it was reported on Wednesday. This week, a Moscow court recognized 13 individuals from the Baltic states and several organizations as "accomplices of Nazi Germany in committing war crimes and crimes against humanity against the Soviets during the Second World War." Among them are Juozas Ambrazevicius, head of the 1941 Lithuanian provisional government, partisan commander Juozas Luksa, writer Bronius Krivickas, who died in the resistance struggle, the Lithuanian Activist Front and the Lithuanian Nationalist Union. The Moscow court said it made the decision after examining archival documents from various Russian agencies and hearing explanations about the "criminal actions" of the aforementioned individuals and organizations from Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia. Lithuania's military has repeatedly said that the country's historical memory policy attracts the attention of Russian propaganda.
